questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Flux of a Vector Field Through a Tilted Plane
questions.problem:
Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨x,\,y,\,2z⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined in Cartesian coordinates as $z=2x+3y$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 1.$ Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ with respect to the upward-pointing unit normal vector $n.$

*Hint: You're given that the fundamental vector product of $S$ with respect to its canonical parametrization is $||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||=\sqrt{14}.$*
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z=2x+3y$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨-2,\,-3,\,1⟩}_{⏟}}_{\overset{~}{n}}=0,\,\text{or}\,⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨2,\,3,\,-1⟩}_{⏟}}_{-\overset{~}{n}}=0.
$$

Since we require an upward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is positive. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\overset{~}{n}=⟨-2,\,-3,\,1⟩.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨-2,\,-3,\,1⟩}{\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+(-3)^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{14}}⟨-2,\,-3,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $z=2x+3y$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨x,\,y,\,2z⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{14}}⟨-2,\,-3,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{14}}⟨x,\,y,\,4x+6y⟩\cdot ⟨-2,\,-3,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{14}}(-2x-3y+4x+6y) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{14}}(2x+3y).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\frac{1}{\sqrt{14}}(2x+3y)\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{\sqrt{14}}(2x+3y)\cdot ||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{\sqrt{14}}(2x+3y)\cdot \sqrt{14}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{\cancel{\sqrt{14}}}(2x+3y)\cdot \cancel{\sqrt{14}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2x+3y\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}2x+3y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[{x}^{2}+3xy]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}1+3y\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[y+\frac{3}{2}{y}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨4y,\,5x,\,2z⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined in Cartesian coordinates as $z=3$ for $1\le x\le 2$ and $1\le y\le 3.$ Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ with respect to the upward-pointing unit normal vector $n.$
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

For the surface $z=3$ for  $1\le x\le 2$ and $1\le y\le 3,$ the upward-pointing unit normal vector is

$$
n=⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=3$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨4y,\,5x,\,2z⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨4y,\,5x,\,6⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}6\,\text{d}S \\  & =6{∬}_{D}\,\text{d}A \\  & =6{\int }_{1}^{3}{\int }_{1}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =6{\int }_{1}^{3}\text{d}y{\int }_{1}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =6\cdot (3-1)\cdot (2-1) \\  & =12\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Flux of a Vector Field Through a Tilted Plane
questions.problem:
Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨-\frac{{y}^{2}+1}{2},\,\frac{{x}^{2}+1}{2},\,z-1⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined in Cartesian coordinates as $z=2x-2y+1$ for $-1\le x\le 0$ and $0\le y\le 1.$ Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ with respect to the upward-pointing unit normal vector $n.$

*Hint: You're given that the fundamental vector product of $S$ with respect to its canonical parametrization is $||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||=3.$*
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z=2x-2y+1$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨-2,\,2,\,1⟩}_{⏟}}_{\overset{~}{n}}=1,\,\text{or}\,⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨2,\,-2,\,-1⟩}_{⏟}}_{-\overset{~}{n}}=-1.
$$

Since we require an upward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is positive. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\overset{~}{n}=⟨-2,\,2,\,1⟩.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨-2,\,2,\,1⟩}{\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨-2,\,2,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $z=2x-2y+1$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨-\frac{{y}^{2}+1}{2},\,\frac{{x}^{2}+1}{2},\,z-1⟩\cdot \frac{1}{3}⟨-2,\,2,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨-\frac{{y}^{2}+1}{2},\,\frac{{x}^{2}+1}{2},\,2x-2y⟩\cdot ⟨-2,\,2,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}({y}^{2}+1+{x}^{2}+1+2x-2y) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[({y}^{2}-2y+1)+({x}^{2}+2x+1)] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[(x+1)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\frac{1}{3}[(x+1)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}]\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{3}[(x+1)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}]\cdot ||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{3}[(x+1)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}]\cdot 3\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{\cancel{3}}[(x+1)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}]\cdot \cancel{3}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}[(x+1)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}]\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{1}[(x+1)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}]\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{[(x+1)^{2}\cdot y+\frac{(y-1)^{3}}{3}]}_{y=0}^{y=1}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}[(x+1)^{2}+\frac{1}{3}]\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{(x+1)^{3}}{3}+\frac{x}{3}]}_{-1}^{0} \\  & =[\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{3}] \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Flux of a Vector Field Through a Horizontal Plane
questions.problem: Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨z,\,z,\,4xy⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined in Cartesian coordinates as $z=1$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 1.$ Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ with respect to the *downward*-pointing unit normal vector $n.$
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is a continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

For the surface $z=1$ for  $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 1,$ the downward-pointing unit normal vector is

$$
n=⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=1$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨z,\,z,\,4xy⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,1,\,4xy⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =-4xy.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}(-4xy)\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-4xy)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}(-4xy)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}2y\,\text{d}y{\int }_{0}^{1}2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{[{y}^{2}]}_{0}^{1}\cdot {[{x}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Flux of a Vector Field Through a Tilted Plane
questions.problem:
Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨3x,\,2z,\,y-2⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined in Cartesian coordinates as $z=2x-y+1$ for $0\le x\le 4$ and $0\le y\le 1.$ Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ with respect to the *downward*-pointing unit normal vector $n.$

*Hint: You're given that the fundamental vector product of $S$ with respect to its canonical parametrization is $||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||=\sqrt{6}.$*
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z=2x-y+1$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨-2,\,1,\,1⟩}_{⏟}}_{-\overset{~}{n}}=1,\,\text{or}\,⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨2,\,-1,\,-1⟩}_{⏟}}_{\overset{~}{n}}=-1.
$$

Since we require a downward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is negative. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\overset{~}{n}=⟨2,\,-1,\,-1⟩.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨2,\,-1,\,-1⟩}{\sqrt{{2}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}⟨2,\,-1,\,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $z=2x-y+1$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨3x,\,2z,\,y-2⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}⟨2,\,-1,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}⟨3x,\,4x-2y+2,\,y-2⟩\cdot ⟨2,\,-1,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(6x-(4x-2y+2)-(y-2)) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(2x+y).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(2x+y)\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(2x+y)\cdot ||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(2x+y)\cdot \sqrt{6}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{\cancel{\sqrt{6}}}(2x+y)\cdot \cancel{\sqrt{6}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2x+y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{4}(2x+y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[{x}^{2}+xy]}_{x=0}^{x=4}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(4y+16)\,\text{d}y \\  & =[2{y}^{2}+16y]_{0}^{1} \\  & =18\end{aligned}
$$
